OET APRIL 2015

PHYSIOTHERAPY

SETTING Suburban Physiotherapy Clinic

PATIENT You are 49 years old, overweight and have recently been diagnosed with
empnysema, which causes breathlessness, increased phlegm and coughing. You
nave been smoking for 30 years and refuse to quit, even though you know that it
makes the condition worse. You have reduced the number of cigarettes you
smoke each day. The doctor has referred you for physiotherapy to help manage
the condition.

TASK e Answer the physiotherapist’s questions about your smoking habits: you smoke
between 10 and 15 cigarettes a day now. You used to smoke about 20 a day.

e Explain that you feel breathless and go into a coughing fit anytime you have to
run or go upstairs.

e Find out how physiotherapy can help with your breathing and coughing.

e Admit that you need to stop smoking but maintain that this is difficult to do as
you have been smoking a very long time.

emphysema, which cau
He/she has been smokin

TASK e Ask how much the patient smokes and when he/she experiences
breathlessness.

e Educate the patient about chronic pulmonary disease (lung condition involving
shortness of breath, etc.) and how it can affect him/her (e.g., limits airflow to
lungs, etc.).

e Suggest exercises that will help to allow the lungs to work easier (e.g., lean
against wall with arms folded above head, etc.).

e Discuss ways to ease the coughing (e.g., sucking on ice, relaxed breathing, etc.).

e Encourage the patient to work towards stopping smoking entirely.

OET APRIL 2015

PHYSIOTHERAPY

SING Hospital Rehabilitation Unit

PATIENT You are an elderly patient who was knocked down by a car recently and your thigh
| bone broke in three places. It has been repaired with a rod, and you are now
having to learn to walk with it. You are not sure whether it will always be so difficult
and painful. You also want to know whether you will ever be able to walk without
the aid of a frame or a stick again.

| TASK e Express frustration that the recovery process is so painful and difficult.

e Find out how long it will take for the pain to ease, and whether you will ever be
pain-free.

e Find out how soon you will be able to live independently again.
e Ask about the physiotherapy routine and find out how long it will continue after

you're discharged from hospital. You are concerned that you find it boring and
you don't see much progress so far.

OET APRIL 2015
CANDIDATE CARD NO. 1 PHYSIOTHERAPY
SETTING Hospital Rehabilitation Unit
PHYSIO This elderly patient has had a fractured femur caused by being knocked down by a

car. It was subsequently treated with ORIF (open reduction internal fixation). You

have to assist him/her to learn to walk again, initially supported by a walking frame.
He/she is finding it difficult, painful and exasperating. After discharge, the treatment |
will continue on a twice-weekly basis.

TASK e Be sympathetic but encourage the patient to continue with his/her recovery plan
despite the pain.

e Reassure him/her that both the pain and difficulty will diminish.

e Answer any questions regarding the long-term prognosis and independent
living (e.g., recovery time depends on the specific injury and may take months;
physiotherapy is essential to regain mobility and strength, etc.).

Outline the physiotherapy routine both while he/she is in hospital and after
discharge (e.g., stretching and flexing to increase range of movement
progressing to simple weight-bearing exercises and gait training, etc.).

HERAPY

SETTING Suburban Physiotherapy Clinic

PATIENT You hurt your left ankle yesterday while playing soccer with your friends (you play
once a week). You turned suddenly and heard a snap. You felt pain immediately
and decided to sit out the rest of the game, and apply ice to the ankle. The last
time this happened it was only a sprain. However, this time it is more painful than
you remember and you cannot put weight on it.

TASK ° Tell the physiotherapist how the injury occurred. Explain that you applied ice and
have been taking pain relievers and anti-inflammatories.

e Answer the physiotherapist’s questions about injuries to your ankle: you have
been playing soccer for five years and you have sprained your left ankle¢wice in
the last two years (the most recent was a year ago).

e Appear dissatisfied with the physiotherapist's referral for X-rays. Insist that you
want treatment for the pain and swelling. 4

e Find out what the difference is between treatment of a sprained ankle and
treatment of a broken ankle.

PHYSIOTHERAP

SETTING Suburban Physiotherapy Clinic

PHYSIO This patient hurt his/her left ankle yesterday while playing soccer. He/she turned
suddenly and heard a snap. The ankle is swollen, red, bruised and painful. The
patient is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He/she thinks it is a sprain.-You
suspect a fracture or break.

TASK ° Find out how the injury occurred and what the patient did to alleviate the pain.
¢ Discuss other injuries the patient may have had to the ankle and when they
occurred (é.g., sprains, etc.). i
Refer the patient for X-rays and explain why you are doing this.
e Maintain that you cannot prescribe treatment until the X-rays are returned but
suggest ways to alleviate the pain and swelling (€.g., rest, ice, etc.).
e Explain the difference between treatment of a sprained ankle and treatment of a

broken ankle (e.g., fracture requires immobilisation, recovery will take longer,
etc.). .

Hospital Rehabilitation Unit

You are a middle-aged patient who was admitted to hospital after a stroke, which
has affected one side of your body. Your speech is slurred and you are aware that
you are dribbling. When you looked in the mirror, you could see that your face was
droopy on one side. You can now sit and stand with assistance, and have got
some movement back in your limbs. You are scared and depressed.

e Find out exactly what has happened to you, and what this means. ©

Ask: "Will | be like this forever? Am | going to be an invalid? Will | ever be
back to normal?"

Explain to the physiotherapist your fears and embarrassment at being like this.

¢ Find out what the treatment involves, and for how Jong it will continue.

Ask the physiotherapist what help is available for coping at home after you are
discharged.

Hospital Rehabilitation Unit

This middle-aged patient was admitted to hospital following a cerebrovascular
accident (CVA) that has resulted in hemiparesis. Speech is possible, although
slurred, and he/she is now able to sit and stand with assistance. There has been
some return of function in the limbs. He/she is now in the rehabilitation ward and is
ready to commence physiotherapy to restore as much function as possible.
Because the CVA was not very dense, the prognosis is quite good.

° Explain what happened to the patient and what this means.

¢ Assure him/her that the prognosis is quite good.
‘

¢ Explain what the therapy will involve and for how long it will continue (e.g.,
mobilisation, etc.).

© Outline the facilities that can be provided at home if necessary (e.g., handrails,

OET MAY 2015

SETTING Suburban Physiotherapy Clinic

PATIENT You are a 63-year-old office worker and have cervical spondylosis (osteoarthritis of
the neck). It feels like your movement is becoming restricted, you cannot fully turn
your head to the left and sometimes you hear a clicking noise when you do. The
pain is waking you at night. You have worked in a busy office for 30 years,
answering phones and typing. The doctor has prescribed you medication for the
inflammation and pain, and has referred you to see the physiotherapist.

TASK ¢ Explain that you type and answer the phone at work, and that this is when you
experience the most discomfort. You rest your phone between your neck and
shoulders.

e Reveal that you lean forward often when you are typing as sometimes you cannot
see the letters on the screen properly.

e Find out if there is anything you can do for the discomfort in your neck.

e Agree to try the change of positioning and exercises.

° Question the advice to remain active. You believe that it will make the neck pain
worse.

e Find out what can be done about your disrupted sleep.

CANDIDATE CARD NO. 2 PHYSIOTHERAPY

SETTING

PHYSIO

TASK

Suburban Physiotherapy Clinic

This 63-year-old office worker with cervical spondylosis (osteoarthritis of the neck)
is experiencing restricted movement when turning the head to the left and is
waking frequently at night due to the pain. The doctor has prescribed medication
for the inflammation and pain and referred the patient to you.

e Find out about the patient’s everyday tasks at work and neck positioning.

¢ Suggest the patient avoid leaning forward and holding the phone between the
neck and shoulders, and recommend better postural positioning.

e Recommend the patient see an optometrist for his/her vision problems and use a
headpiece for the phone.

Describe exercises to Improve strength and mobility of the neck (e.g., looking up
and down, side to side, etc.).

e Encourage the patient to remain active.

e Recommend something to help ease the patient’s neck while sleeping (e.g., a
cervical pillow, etc.).

Suburban Clinic

You are 28 years old. You recently went on a skiing holiday overseas, during which
you sustained a knee injury. You heard a popping noise, your knee immediately
became swollen and tender, and it was wobbly to walk on. You are quite worried
that you have done some permanent damage and will never be able to ski again.

Answer the physiotherapist’s questions about how the injury occurred.

If asked, explain that you do not experience any locking or catching sensations.
Find out what the therapist thinks has happened.

Ask if you are likely to recover completely so you can ski again.

Ask what you can do to hasten the recovery.

Find out if there are any exercises that would be helpful now.

OET MAY 2015

CANDIDATE CARD NO. 1 PHYSIOTHERAPY

SETTING

PHYSIO

TASK

Suburban Clinic

A 28-year-old patient has presented with a knee injury that was sustained while

skiing overseas. He/she reports an audible pop, immediate swelling and

tenderness, and a feeling of instability. You suspect a torn anterior cruciate

ligament (ACL). You perform a medial-lateral grind test to rule out meniscus
damage.

Find out how the injury was sustained.

Ask about locking or catching sensations to rule out meniscal tears.

Explain your diagnosis to the patient (e.g., a tear in the tissue which joins the
thigh bone to the shin bone, etc.).

Reassure him/her about the likelinood of full recovery.

Give advice regarding appropriate treatment (e.g., rest, ice, compression,
elevation, etc.).

Outline any exercises that may be useful now or at a later stage (e.g., exercises
to strengthen the muscles around the knee, cycling on a stationary bicycle, etc.).

© Cambridge Boxhill Language Assessment MAY 2015

ROLEPLAYER CARD NO. 1 PHYSIOTHERAPY

SETTING Hospital

PATIENT You have just had your dislocated shoulder relocated under local anaesthetic in
hospital. You incurred this injury while playing baseball with your nephews on the
weekend. When bowling, you felt severe pain in your right shoulder, extending
down your arm. You were unable to lift your arm up away from your body. You feel
numb over right shoulder. You are now scheduled to speak to the physiotherapist
about further management.

TASK ¢ Find out what has actually happened during the injury.

e Ask the physiotherapist the following questions:
- What is a dislocation?
- What did the relocation involve?
- What treatment will you need to have now?
- How will the pain be managed?
- Will you need to keep your arm in a sling?
- What benefits will physiotherapy have?

SETTING Hospital

PHYSIO A patient has just been treated in hospital for a dislocated shoulder (with reduction
of the shoulder using local injection of anaesthetic). The injury was incurred while
bowling during a baseball game on the weekend. The pain in the shoulder extends
down the right arm, and there is a query about numbness over the deltoid region.

TASK e Explain the shoulder injury to the patient.
e Answer the patient’s questions about dislocation.
Explain what the treatment involves and outline how the treated shoulder will be
managed.
Ask about the pain — intensity, location.
Answer questions about pain reduction.
Answer questions about the use of a sling.
Explain what physiotherapy can do, and what it will involve.

SETTING Suburban Physiotherapy Clinic
PATIENT You are a 50-year-old avid kayaker and cyclist. Last week you began to experience
numbness in your left foot after riding on a different bike for 40 kilometres. You

think this may be due to the bike. You have not injured your back and have never
had problems with it before.

TASK e Inform the physiotherapist that you have not experienced any weakness or
paralysis.

e Answer the physiotherapist’s question about your back and ask why this is
relevant.

° Ask if there is anything else that can cause numbness in the foot.
e Become alarmed. You thought the problem was with the bike.

° Insist that you are sure the problem is with the bike.

OET NOVEMBER 2014
CANDIDATE CARD NO. 2 PHYSIOTHERAPY

SETTING Suburban Physiotherapy Clinic

PHYSIO You are seeing a 50-year-old kayaker and cyclist. The patient began to experience
numbness in his/her left foot after riding on a different bicycle for 40 kilometres. The
patient believes the new bike is the cause of the numbness.

TASK e Find out if the patient is experiencing weakness or paralysis.

° Ask if the patient has had problems with his/her back.

e In simple terms, explain that a nerve root or spinal nerve injury can refer
numbness to a distal area that it supplies, like the foot.

© Give examples of other possible causes of numbness in the foot (e.g., Morton’s
neuroma, pressure on nerve between 2/3 or 3/4 toes, Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome,
etc.).

e Agree that the problem could be with the bike and give examples of how the
bike could cause the numbness (e.g., positioning of seat/pedals/length of frame,
position when riding, etc.).

e Assure the patient that it is necessary to rule out other physical causes initially.

© Cambridge Boxhill Language Assessment NOVEMBER 2014

OET AUGUST 2015

ROLEPLAYER CARD NO. 1 PHYSIOTHERAPY

SETTING Hospital Physiotherapy Department

PATIENT You are a 68-year-old widow/widower waiting for a hip replacement operation. You
have been told you may have to wait another 12 months. The surgeon has sent
you for physiotherapy assessment and management. Your house has six steps at
the front and back with no railing and you live alone. You were given non-steroidal
anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for the pain.

TASK ¢ Complain about the amount of time you will be on the waiting list for a hip
replacement operation.

e When prompted, explain that walking and climbing stairs make the pain worse
and tablets (NSAIDs) from the doctor make it better.

e Answer the physiotherapist’s questions: You don’t drive and are finding it hard to
walk to the shops. You aren’t confident on public transport. You are scared of
slipping in the bathtub under the shower, so you have been cutting down on
showers. .

e Tell the physiotherapist that you are having difficulty cleaning and cooking. You
expect your daughter-in-law to come over after work to help, but she is resisting.

e Resist discussion about moving to supported accommodation — in your opinion
your family should be responsible for your care.

SETTING

Hospital Physiotherapy Department

PHYSIO Your patient is a 68-year-old widow/widower who lives alone and is on a waiting list
for a hip replacement operation. He/she may have to wait for another 12 months.
The surgeon has sent him/her for physiotherapy assessment and management.
The patient has been prescribed non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

TASK e Reassure the patient that physiotherapy can help to ease the discomfort while
waiting for the hip replacement operation.

e Ask about activities that aggravate and ease the condition.

e Find out about the patient’s mobility (e.g., driving, walking to shops, public
transport, showering, etc.) and needs at home (e.g., cleaning, cooking, etc.).

e Explain how physiotherapy can help the patient to become more mobile.

Discuss the possibility of moving the patient into supported accommodation to
ease the burden on the patient’s family.

SETTING Suburban Physiotherapy Clinic
PATIENT You are 49 years old and work as an event planner. You are experiencing pain and

stiffness in the fingers of your right hand and a bit of pain and stiffness in the left
hand. You are having difficulty managing day to day tasks and work, and are
feeling a bit tired. Your fingers are particularly stiff in the morning for a few hours.
You have come to the physiotherapist for help to manage the condition.

TASK ¢ Answer the physiotherapist’s questions about the symptoms and mention that
| you have been experiencing a bit of pain and stiffness in your toes as well.

¢ Become concerned when the physiotherapist tells you that you might have
rheumatoid arthritis. Ask the physiotherapist to explain what the condition is.

® Continue to express concern. You do not know how you will manage all your
tasks at work.

e Find out how you can be sure you have this condition.
